块28–42及附录A/B：负log-Dice可以拆成前景匹配与区域大小项；多类区域项`sum_k log(p_hat_k+y_hat_k)`是关于预测比例单纯形的凹函数，最小值可在最大GT类别所对应的一个顶点达到。二类foreground-only区域项`log(p_hat_fg+y_hat_fg)`偏好更小预测前景。**这说的是拆分后区域项的偏好，不是完整Dice loss的全局最优必然全背景。**完整匹配项仍鼓励GT前景概率为1；线性Dice与log-Dice的界和同理约束，不代表二者训练梯度/结果相同。

块20/32/156/195的CE按类别分别除以该类GT大小；附录A.3式20又是逐像素均值CE。不能忽略这种记法/权重差异，将其Jensen界或隐含项数值逐字套到本项目`binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(..., reduction='mean')`。当前模型还采用整batch foreground-only Dice、平滑常数1、三尺度权重4/7、2/7、1/7；不等于原文所有理论条件和实现。空GT使若干原文`1/|Omega_k|`及log y项无定义，需限定有正类GT；我们保留空样本/域，不丢弃以制造优势。

块45–58/170–190的CE信息论观点使用生成式解释、Monte-Carlo熵估计和Bayes关系；不是任意未校准神经概率上的无条件统计保证。作者提出CE加显式L1/KL区域比例正则，缓解不同区域贡献的失衡。比例一致本身不保证位置/病灶正确：相同体积可完全错位，因此不能用RVE改善替代Dice、recall和TP>0。

0 title ABSTRACT
1 p Inner ear segmentation supports the diagnosis and treatment planning of auditory‐related disorders such as Meniere's disease. However, manual annotation of inner ear structures on MR images is both time‐consuming and labor‐intensive. To address this limitation, we developed a deep learning method that takes T2‐weighted MR images as input and segments the inner ear into three subregions: the cochlear basal turn, the cochlear mid‐to‐apical turn, and the vestibule including the semicircular canals. A total of 74 three‐dimensional (3D) T2‐weighted MR images were retrospectively collected and divided into 50 training cases and 24 internal test cases. In addition, eight MR images from the publicly available Vestibular‐Schwannoma‐SEG dataset were used as an independent external test set. Ground‐truth segmentations for both the internal and external datasets were manually annotated by an experienced radiologist. A 3D transformer‐based deep learning model was trained using these annotated data. To further improve segmentation performance, particularly for the thin and intricate semicircular canals, a label‐preserving data augmentation strategy was introduced and compared with a conventional data augmentation approach. Segmentation performance was evaluated using quantitative and qualitative assessments. Quantitative evaluation included the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), Intersection over union (IoU), and Hausdorff distance (HD). On the internal test set, the proposed method achieved a mean DSC of 0.905 (vs. 0.904), a mean IoU of 0.828 (vs. 0.824), and a mean HD of 2.75 (vs. 3.04) compared with the conventional augmentation approach. On the external dataset, the proposed method demonstrated larger improvements, achieving a mean DSC of 0.919 (vs. 0.847), a mean IoU of 0.852 (vs. 0.738), and a mean HD of 3.92 (vs. 4.45). These results demonstrate that the proposed label‐preserving data augmentation method improves the robustness and accuracy of inner ear subregion segmentation, particularly for thin and intricate structures.
2 p Keywords: deep learning, inner ear, MRI, segmentation, semicircular canals
3 p A deep learning segmentation model was proposed for automated inner ear subregion segmentation using 3D T2‐weighted MRI. A transformer‐based model with label‐preserving data augmentation improves delineation of thin and complex structures such as the semicircular canals. Automated and reliable inner ear subregion segmentation may support quantitative assessment and aid diagnosis for auditory‐related disorders such as Meniere's disease.
4 title Introduction
5 p The contrast enhancement of the inner ear, an essential component of the auditory system, is frequently evaluated in clinical diagnoses of disorders such as Meniere's disease, sudden sensorineural hearing loss, and vestibular neuritis [1, 2, 3]. In these diagnostic processes, delayed post‐contrast MR images are commonly employed because the degree of contrast enhancement serves as a key diagnostic marker [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9].
6 p Segmentation of the inner ear fluid space can serve as a mask to enable planimetric [10] or volumetric measurements [11] providing a more comprehensive and quantitative assessment of enhancement patterns over visual or region of interest‐based analysis. The inner ear consists of the cochlea, vestibule, and three semicircular canals, each with distinct functions and associated clinical symptoms when affected, and contrast enhancement patterns observed in specific subregions have been shown to correlate with distinct clinical parameters [12] and may possess differing prognostic value [13] or even differentiate various types of hearing loss [14]. When evaluating Meniere's disease, endolymphatic hydrops is visually graded separately in the cochlear and vestibular compartments [15]. Therefore, subregion‐based segmentation may offer potential for further refinement of diagnostic and prognostic assessments [16]. In addition, segmentation of the inner ear fluid space can also be used for morphometric analysis [17] or serve as a mask for signal intensity measurement [18] and radiomic analysis [18]. However, manual annotation for this purpose is both time‐consuming and labor‐intensive [19]. Consequently, several studies have focused on developing automatic segmentation methods for inner ear structures [10, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26].
7 p Previous studies have investigated algorithm‐based methods for inner ear segmentation [20, 26]. For example, Todd et al. examined a region‐growing algorithm [20], but this approach suffers from limited robustness because it is sensitive to data resolution variations and relies heavily on seed point placement, which can lead to inconsistent results. Similarly, Xianfen et al. explored a narrow‐band level set method [26] but encountered challenges in segmenting complex structures, such as the semicircular canals, and in achieving full automation. Atlas‐based segmentation has also been examined [21]; however, this technique depends greatly on the accuracy of expert segmentations used to construct the atlas, and the inverse transformation process necessary to restore the segmentation to its original shape can introduce distortions.
8 p Recently, advancements in deep learning have led to an increasing number of studies on inner ear segmentation [10, 22, 23, 24, 25]. Nonetheless, prior deep learning‐based approaches have either lacked full automation [22] or did not segment the inner ear into detailed subregions [23, 24, 25], which are essential for more comprehensive analysis. Although Cho et al. differentiated between the cochlea and vestibule, their study omitted the semicircular canals [10].
9 p To address these limitations, we developed a fully automated, deep learning‐based method for subregion segmentation of the entire inner ear. Our method delineates the inner ear into three regions: the cochlear basal turn, the cochlear mid‐to‐apical turn, and the vestibule, including the semicircular canals. Moreover, previous studies have reported difficulties in accurately segmenting the semicircular canals, which are thin and complex structures within the inner ear, primarily due to the partial volume effect [26]. To overcome this challenge, we propose a simple augmentation method that has the potential to enhance training for intricate and thin structures such as the semicircular canals.
10 title Materials and Methods
11 p This retrospective study was approved by the local institutional review board, and the requirement for written informed consent was waived.
12 title Study Population
13 p A total of 74 ear MRI examinations were collected from the hospital PACS system. All images were anonymized and then divided into a training set of 50 MRI examinations and a temporally independent test set of 24 MRI examinations. Additionally, eight T2‐weighted images from the publicly available Vestibular‐Schwannoma‐SEG collection, released on The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA), were included as independent test data [27].
14 title MRI Acquisition
15 title Internal Dataset
16 p For training and evaluation of the inner ear subregion segmentation model, 3D T2‐weighted images were collected. All images were acquired using a fast spin echo sequence at a 3‐T MRI system (Signa Architect, GE Healthcare, Milwaukee, WI, USA) with a 48‐channel head coil. The sequence parameters were as follows: repetition time = 1500 ms, echo time = 80 ms, in‐plane resolution = 0.3125 mm, slice thickness = 0.4 mm, field of view = 160 × 160 × 20.8 mm3, and acquisition time = 6 min 45 s [28].
17 title External Dataset
18 p Validation was conducted on an external public dataset with varying imaging protocols and contrasts to assess the generalizability of the trained model. T2‐weighted images from the Vestibular‐Schwannoma‐SEG collection were acquired by a 1.5‐T MRI system (Magnetom Avanto, Siemens, Erlangen, Germany) with a single‐channel head coil. The sequence parameters were either a constructive interference steady‐state sequence (repetition time = 9.4 ms, echo time = 4.23 ms, in‐plane resolution = 0.47 mm, slice thickness = 1.5 mm, and field of view = 210.56 × 210.56 × 120 mm3) or a fast spin echo sequence (repetition time = 750 ms, echo time = 121 ms, in‐plane resolution = 0.55 mm, slice thickness = 1.5 mm, and field of view = 211.2 × 211.2 × 60 mm3) [27].
19 title Ground‐Truth Determination
20 p The ground‐truth segmentations were created by an experienced radiologist. As shown in Figure 1, the inner ear was divided into three subregions: the cochlear basal turn, the cochlear mid‐to‐apical turn, and the vestibule, including the semicircular canals.

22 title Label‐Preserving Data Augmentation
23 p In this study, we observed that conventional augmentation techniques, particularly rotation and scaling, often lead to the loss or distortion of labels. This issue is most pronounced in the semicircular canals, the thinnest parts of our labels (see red arrowheads and green circles in Figure 2a). When transforming labels, nearest‐neighbor interpolation is typically used to maintain their discreteness. However, this method is inadequate for thin structures like the semicircular canals, where there is a high risk of mistakenly assigning background voxels to regions that should belong to the foreground. These interpolation errors can degrade the model's ability to accurately segment thin structures, ultimately reducing its overall performance.

25 p To address this issue, we propose a label‐preserving augmentation method that applies geometric transformations and their inverses sequentially, but only to the input images, while keeping the labels unchanged [29, 30]. The overall workflow of the proposed method, demonstrated for rotation and scaling, is illustrated in Figure 2b. Even after applying the inverse transformations, the resulting images exhibit alterations due to interpolation in finite space. However, because the underlying structure is preserved, the original labels can still be used without modification. For rotation, a random degree of θ and its inverse, −θ, were applied sequentially along the x‐axis. Similarly, random scaling and its inverse were applied in sequence. We evaluated the effectiveness of our proposed method by comparing it with a conventional augmentation approach (Figure 2a), hereafter referred to as the baseline method, which applies transformations to both images and labels without reverting the input image to its original form.
26 title Segmentation Model and Training Procedure
27 p In our study, fully automated end‐to‐end segmentation was performed using Swin UNETR [31], a 3D U‐shaped model based on the Swin‐transformer. As shown in Figure 3, the model received heavily T2‐weighted MR images as input, which were randomly cropped to a consistent size of 96×96×32 voxels. The corresponding ground‐truth segmentations, matched in size and location, were used as labels. To reduce the risk of overfitting, we applied various data augmentation techniques, including random Gaussian noise addition, random smoothing and sharpening, and random flipping along the horizontal, vertical, and depth axes, during the training phase for both the baseline and the proposed method. Notably, while all other augmentation strategies were applied identically, the rotation and scaling operations were implemented differently between the baseline and proposed models, as outlined in Figure 2. We utilized a combined loss function, incorporating both Dice loss [32] and cross‐entropy loss [33] with equal weighting. The model's parameters were optimized using the AdamW optimizer [34], with a learning rate of 10−4 and a weight decay of 10−3, over a training period of 500 epochs to ensure convergence of the loss function. The models were implemented using PyTorch version 2.1.2 [35] and the MONAI version 1.3.0 [36]. All training was conducted on a single NVIDIA Titan XP GPU with 12 GB of memory.

29 title Post Processing
30 p The output from our model was a four‐channel probability map, comprising probability distributions for one background and three distinct foreground elements. To eliminate false positives, we first generated masks for the foreground elements by applying connected‐component labeling to a thresholded foreground probability map derived from the model's output. The corresponding foreground probability maps were then multiplied by these masks, effectively removing false positives. Subsequently, we refined the background probability map using the masked foreground probability maps. The final segmentation was obtained by applying the argmax function across all probability maps. This systematic approach effectively preserved thin structures, such as the semicircular canals, while efficiently eliminating false positives.
31 title Evaluation
32 p The segmentation results were evaluated using both an internal dataset (N = 24) and an external dataset (N = 8). Inner ear structures on the left and right sides were identified and analyzed independently, with metrics calculated separately for each side, yielding 48 samples for the internal dataset and 16 samples for the external dataset. The evaluation included both quantitative and qualitative analyses.
33 p For the quantitative analysis, we calculated the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), Intersection over Union (IoU), and Hausdorff Distance (HD) for each region (the cochlear basal turn, the cochlear mid‐to‐apical turn, and the vestibule, including the semicircular canals), focusing exclusively on the foreground. The distributions of these metrics were visualized using box plots to provide a clear and comprehensive overview. Additionally, t‐tests were performed to compare the segmentations obtained from the baseline method with those generated by the proposed method for each region, with a p‐value < 0.05 indicating statistical significance. For the qualitative analysis, two experienced radiologists visually assessed the accuracy and reliability of the segmentations.

52 title Discussion
53 p In this study, we developed a model for inner ear subregion segmentation, dividing the inner ear into three regions: the cochlear basal turn, cochlear mid‐to‐apical turn, and the vestibule, including the semicircular canals. Additionally, we proposed a label‐preserving augmentation method designed to improve the segmentation of complex and thin structures, with a specific focus on the semicircular canals.
54 p Both quantitative and qualitative evaluations on the internal and the external datasets demonstrated that the proposed label‐preserving augmentation method significantly improved performance, particularly for thin structures such as the semicircular canals. The vestibule, including the semicircular canals, which was the main focus of this study, showed improved performance across all metrics compared to the baseline. Minor improvements were also observed in other regions, further supporting the overall effectiveness of the proposed method. Although the visual assessment revealed clear improvements with the proposed method, the statistical analysis on the internal test set did not reach significance. This discrepancy may stem from the limitations of overlap‐based metrics such as DSC and IoU, which are less sensitive to the topology or continuity of small, thin anatomical structures. To confirm that the observed improvements were not architecture‐dependent, we additionally applied the proposed augmentation strategy to a U‐Net architecture [37], which has been commonly used in previous inner ear segmentation studies [25, 26]. Our proposed method achieved improved performance compared to conventional augmentation in both Swin UNETR and U‐Net, demonstrating its generalizability (Figure S1 and Tables S1 and S2). In addition, Swin UNETR is recommended as the backbone network due to its strong overall performance compared to U‐Net architectures, which do not incorporate transformers.
55 p A notable difference between the external dataset and the training data lies in the z‐axis resolution, with the external data exhibiting significantly lower resolution in this dimension. Despite this challenge, our proposed method demonstrated strong performance in segmenting the inner ear, which is characterized by intricate and thin structures that are more susceptible to distortion at lower resolutions. In addition, although the external dataset included the constructive interference steady‐state sequence, which exhibits mixed T1/T2 contrast slightly different from the T2‐weighted contrast in the training set, our method still maintained strong performance. These results highlight the robustness of the proposed label‐preserving augmentation method, showing that it handles variations in resolution more effectively than the baseline and underscoring its potential for broader applicability to datasets with varying image quality.
56 p Similar to our study, previous research has addressed label distortion caused by nearest‐neighbor interpolation by applying linear interpolation to labels and utilizing soft labels [38]. However, since linear interpolation produces labels with continuous values, such methods are limited to binary segmentation. In contrast, our proposed method shows potential for application to multiclass segmentation, offering greater versatility and broader applicability.
57 p The automatic generation of accurate inner ear subregion segmentation, enhanced by the proposed method, can facilitate the evaluation of various inner ear disorders without the need for expert labor. By enabling the precise quantification of contrast enhancement within each of the three distinct regions (the cochlear basal turn, cochlear mid‐to‐apical turn, and the vestibule, including the semicircular canals), this segmentation approach has the potential to contribute to a more accurate diagnosis.
58 title Limitations
59 p This study has several limitations. As shown in Figure 9, when the input image has low contrast, particularly in the semicircular canals, both the baseline and proposed methods struggle to accurately segment the inner ear structure (see yellow arrowheads in Figure 9). Additionally, the validation of our method was limited to rotation and scaling, with rotation confined to the x‐axis. Given the promising results, future work should explore extending this method to other axes of rotation and incorporating additional geometric transformations. Furthermore, it is important to verify the generalizability of the method to other complex or small structures beyond the inner ear, particularly those susceptible to partial volume effects.

61 title Conclusion
62 p In this study, we introduced a deep learning‐based inner ear subregion segmentation method, enhanced by a label‐preserving data augmentation technique. This method delineates the inner ear into three distinct regions: the cochlear basal turn, the cochlear mid‐to‐apical turn, and the vestibule, including the semicircular canals. This approach has the potential to support the diagnosis of inner ear disorders by enabling more precise quantification of regional contrast enhancement.

0 title Abstract
1 title Objectives
2 p Management of patients with vestibular schwannoma (VS) relies on precise tumor size and growth trend evaluation. We introduce and evaluate a novel computer-assisted reporting tool for clinical decision support during multidisciplinary team meetings (MDTMs) for VS patients.
3 title Materials and Methods
4 p Our approach exploits deep learning for tumor segmentation, automating tumor volume, and standard linear measurement extraction. We conducted 2 simulated MDTMs with the same 50 patients evaluated in both arms to compare our proposed approach against the standard process, focusing on its impact on preparation time and decision-making.
5 title Results
6 p Automated reports provided acceptable information for an expert neuroradiologist in 72% of cases, while the remaining 28% required some revision with manual feature extraction. The segmentation models used in this report generation task achieved Dice scores of 0.9392 (±0.0351) for contrast-enhanced T1 and 0.9331 (±0.0354) for T2 MRI in delineating whole tumor regions. The automated computer-assisted reports that included additional tumor information initially extended the neuroradiologist’s preparation time for the MDTM (2 min 54 s [±1 min and 22 s] per case) compared to the standard preparation time (2 min 36 s (±1 min and 5 s] per case). However, the computer-assisted simulated MDTM approach significantly improved (P < .01) MDTM efficiency, with shorter discussion times per patient (1 min 15 s [±0 min and 28 s] per case) compared to standard simulated MDTM (1 min 21 s [±0 min and 44 s] per case).
7 title Discussion
8 p An initial learning curve in interpreting new data measurements is quickly mastered and the enhanced communication of growth patterns and more comprehensive assessments ultimately provides clinicians with the tools to offer patients more personalized care.
9 title Conclusion
10 p This pilot clinical implementation study highlights the potential benefits of integrating automated measurements into clinical decision-making for VS management.
11 p Keywords: vestibular schwannoma, deep learning, segmentation, feature extraction, personalized management
12 title Introduction
13 p Vestibular schwannoma (VS) is a benign brain tumor originating from myelinating Schwann cells within the vestibular division of the vestibulocochlear nerve. The incidence rate of VS is rising.1 In the United Kingdom, the incidence rate is approximately 2.2 per 100 000 people per year2 with some estimates indicating that approximately 1 in 1000 people will be diagnosed with a VS in their lifetime.3 The increasing availability and improved quality of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has resulted in higher proportion of small asymptomatic tumors now being diagnosed. For smaller tumors, expectant management with lifelong imaging is often advised4 with patients proceeding to stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) or conventional open surgery should the tumor demonstrate growth on serial imaging. Even after treatment, patients typically require an extended period of surveillance.
14 p The assessment of VS growth requires a standardized measurement approach.5 The 2001 Consensus Meeting on Reporting Results in Acoustic Neuroma recommends distinguishing intrameatal and extrameatal portions and measuring the largest extrameatal diameter.6 When a tumor is entirely intrameatal, this measurement becomes the maximum whole tumor diameter. For VS treatment decisions, both linear and volumetric measurements are applicable. As per the European Academy of Otology & Neuro-Otology position statement, the criteria for significant VS growth include a >2 mm increase in diameter, a >1.2 cm3 volume change, or a >20% volume change.7 The United Kingdom introduced cancer multidisciplinary team meetings (MDTMs) to ensure uniform high-quality care for all cancer patients, regardless of origin.8 Defining overall growth and growth rate is a key element in determining treatment strategies for patients with VS,4,7 alongside other factors such as absolute size, patient comorbidities, hearing, age, and patient preference. The manual extraction of linear measurements is a time-consuming process that is susceptible to variation and interobserver error.9 Volumetric measurements offer higher sensitivity and precision, but existing methods, including manual or semiautomated tumor segmentation, are labor-intensive, lack standardization and are prone to variability and subjectivity.10,11 Additionally, the lack of readily available standardized software has hindered the adoption of incorporating volumetric measurements into routine clinical practice.
15 p Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a valuable tool in various aspects of VS research. Deep learning and machine learning techniques have been utilized for tumor segmentation,12–14 growth prediction,15,16 surgical outcome prediction,17,18 and Koos grade prediction.19 Previous work has shown that AI tools possess the technical capability to fully automate the detection and segmentation of VS,12,20 and can also delineate the tumor’s intra- and extrameatal components.14 These tools formed the basis for automating the extraction process of both linear and volumetric measurements in this study. Nevertheless, while AI has shown promise in VS management, the assessment of its clinical applicability and its impact on decision-making requires further investigation.
16 p In this study, we developed an automated imaging biomarker report generator that employs deep learning segmentation and computer algorithms for feature extraction and visualization. Each report included longitudinal measurements of the tumor, representative axial views of the tumor, and graphical representations to illustrate changes in both linear and volume measurements. This study assesses the overall process of implementing AI-driven automated reporting methods in a simulated controlled real-world context (Figure 1). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to integrate AI-based outcomes into clinical practice evaluating their impact on clinical decision-making for tumor management.

18 title Materials and methods
19 p To evaluate the impact on standard clinical practice, 2 separate simulated MDTM sessions involving 50 referred patients were conducted in a controlled setting. Decisions made in the simulated MDTMs did not impact patient care. The first session adhered to the standard preparation procedure with manual extraction, while the second session introduced the automated imaging biomarker report.
20 title Datasets
21 p For his retrospective exploratory study, we utilized 2 datasets: KCH MC-RC and UCLH MC-RC, each obtained from different referral centers in London, United Kingdom. UCLH MC-RC was used for internal segmentation model development (training, hyperparameter tuning, and testing), whereas KCH MC-RC was used for external validation during the CAS-MDTM process. Further details can be found in Appendix A.1.
22 title Ethics statement
23 p This study was approved by the NHS Health Research Authority and Research Ethics Committee (18/LO/0532). Because patients were selected retrospectively and the MR images were completely anonymized before analysis, no informed consent was required for the study.
24 title Formation of automated imaging biomarker reports
25 title Deep learning model development
26 p Building on the methodology in Wijethilake et al,14 we adopted a 2-stage approach employing the default 3D full-resolution UNet from the nnU-Net framework (referred to as 3D nnU-Net). Additional information regarding the internal training, hyperparameter tuning and testing sets, methodology and training procedures can be found in Appendices A.1 and A.2 (What we refer to as hyperparameter tuning set is often referred as validation set in the machine learning community. We use the terminology “hyper-parameter tuning” to avoid any ambiguity with regard to our independent external validation set.). There was no overlap in patients between the internal training dataset and the external validation set used in this study’s simulated MDTMs.
27 title Feature extraction and visualization
28 p For the KCH MC-RC dataset, we acquired segmentation masks using the best-performing deep learning models and utilized them in the feature extraction process. The primary linear measurement we extracted for each VS was the maximum tumor diameter. This measurement could be derived from 2 regions: the entire tumor region (DWT) and/or the extrameatal region of the tumor (DEM). When the extrameatal tumor portion was small or negligible, radiologists typically measured the linear dimension for the entire tumor region (combining both intra- and extrameatal regions).
29 p More details about the linear features and selection of the appropriate measurement to present are provided in Appendix A.3. Further, in our previous study,21 we conducted a preliminary evaluation comparing automated and an expert’s manual linear measurements.
30 title Choice of diameter to display to the clinical team
31 p To streamline and simplify the presentation of data for the clinical team, we choose to extract and display only one of these diameters DWT and DEM. The selection of which diameter to present to the users depends on the patient’s operative status and is influenced by the three additional features introduced earlier. For cases that have undergone surgery, we extract the maximum whole tumor diameter. For preoperative cases, we consider 2 subscenarios. The first subscenario occurs when the predicted mask is entirely intracanalicular, meaning only an intrameatal region is present. In this case, the intrameatal region represents the entire tumor, and we extract its maximum diameter. The second subscenario arises when the predicted mask includes an extrameatal portion. We then evaluate three additional features to determine which diameter should be extracted. In this second subscenario, the presented feature is decided using the following algorithm:
32 p IF d(intra,∥) ≥ d(extra,∥)
33 p → use DWT
34 p ELSE
35 p IF d(extra,⊥) >2 mm
36 p → use DEM
37 p ELSE IF d(extra,⊥) ≤2 mm
38 p → use DWT
39 p Additionally, volume measurements were extracted for the intra- and extrameatal regions. Visualization of the axial slice with the maximum D was done using the 3D Slicer software extension with Python.22 Additionally, 3D volume mask of the tumor was visualized. Further, in our previous study,21 we conducted a preliminary evaluation comparing automated and an expert’s manual linear measurements.
40 title Automated generation of the imaging biomarker report
41 p Automated report generation followed 2 key steps: (1) segmentation and (2) feature extraction. For each patient a summary report and an extended version were generated. In the summary report, an MRI axial slice representative of each time point was included, along with the intra-/extrameatal mask, corresponding extrameatal and whole tumor volumes, and maximum D measurement. Volume measurements were not presented if the tumor was present in more than 1 axial slice. The summary report formation details, along with an example report, are provided in Figure 2. Additionally, an extended report is generated with all the measurements and 3D visualizations.

43 title Simulated MDTMs
44 title Preparation for the standard MDTM
45 p The neuroradiologist prepared for the SS-MDTM under time-constrained conditions to replicate clinical MDTM preparation following UK practice guidelines. Linear measurements were extracted from the index, second most recent, and most recent scans for each patient using the Picture Archiving & Communications System (PACS) workstation (Sectra workstation, Sectra AB, Sweden) at King’s College Hospital, London, United Kingdom. For each patient, the neuroradiologist recorded the absolute linear measurements, provided a qualitative description of the tumor, and made judgments regarding tumor growth (change/no change/equivocal) on a structured form. Longitudinal changes were assessed between the index and recent time points and between the second most recent and most recent time points. The starting and finishing times for manual feature extraction for each patient case were recorded. The neuroradiologist’s workload was also assessed using the NASA-TLX scoring system after completing the preparations, that evaluates a task based on 6 dimensions: mental demand, physical demand, temporal demand, performance, effort, and frustration, to provide an overall workload score.23 Higher NASA-TLX scores indicate greater perceived workload and stress associated with the task, reflecting increased cognitive or physical effort required by the user.
46 title Execution of the standard MDTM
47 p The SS-MDTM was conducted with the minimum required attendees, and it took place as a hybrid online-in-person meeting. The simulated skull-base MDTM included 2 skull-base neurosurgeons (N.T., J.S.), 2 clinical oncologists (K.C., O.A.), 2 clinical nurse specialists (A.H., J.D.L.D.S.), and 3 neurosurgical fellows (T.G., A.A., C.S.). Each case was presented to the MDTM by the MDTM coordinator (A.O). The neuroradiologist (S.C.) then presented the tumor measurements and observations, with the tumor displayed on the PACS system through screen sharing. The starting and finishing times of the MDTM were recorded.
48 title Preparation for the CAS-MDTM
49 p The CAS-MDTM was conducted 35 days after the SS-MDTM. To reduce the potential for bias, the order of the 50 cases was altered and randomly assigned. Once again, the neuroradiologist prepared for the CAS-MDTM in a time-constrained environment, this time utilizing the automated report. In this preparation phase, the neuroradiologist evaluated and decided on the acceptance or rejection of automated biomarkers for each patient’s MRI session (time point). This external validation was performed considering the segmentation outcomes provided by the deep learning model, while assessing the robustness of the deep learning-based segmentation model. If a session was rejected, the neuroradiologist manually extracted the linear measurements. The assessments conducted during this process followed the same procedure as in the SS-MDTM, utilizing the index, second most recent, and their most recent scans. The overall growth from the index scan or interval growth from the second most recent scan was documented.7
50 title Execution of the computer-assisted MDTM
51 p The CAS-MDTM followed the same format and impact assessment criteria as the SS-MDTM but introducing an evaluation of volume differences between the scans. CAS-MDTM was held 35 days after the SS-MDTM. Automated reports were distributed to all participants prior to the MDTM and the neuroradiologist (S.C.) presented his observations, referencing either linear or volume measurements as necessary. During the CAS-MDTM, members also referred to the automated report to assist their decision-making.
52 title Results
53 title Deep learning-based segmentation
54 p The segmentation model provided whole tumor Dice scores of 0.8962 (±0.0510) for T2 and 0.8655 (±0.0836) for T1C on the internal testing set after first stage of 2-stage framework. After 2-stage segmentation, the model achieved whole tumor Dice scores of 0.9392 (±0.0351) for T2 and 0.9331 (±0.0354) for T1C, respectively, on the internal testing set. The performance of the segmentation models during the internal testing phase is presented in Appendix B.1.
55 title Sample reports generated through automated imaging biomarker reporting
56 p The report included a visual representation of volume and maximum diameter (D) change, using color coding to indicate growth (red), equivocal growth (orange), and no growth (green). Intra-/extrameatal volumes were displayed in a bar plot, and diameters in a line plot with the x-axis representing time in months. Icons on the graph represented the decisions made after each session, with a guide provided at the bottom of the report. Figure 2 illustrates a report generated using our proposed methodology. It also demonstrates a case where the tumor shows an initial increase in size following SRS, a known posttreatment effect that does not necessarily indicate treatment failure or disease progression.
57 title Neuroradiological preparation for the CAS-MDTM
58 p In 72% of cases (36 patients), the automatically generated segmentations and linear/volume measurements were accepted and used for assessing tumor growth by the neuroradiologist (see “Sample Reports Generated Through Automated Imaging Biomarker Reporting”). The neuroradiologist’s observations, combining manual and automated measurements, were presented to the MDTM and in 12 cases the neuroradiologist chose to only present the automatically generated volume measurements provided in the summary report. For 16% of cases (8 patients), 1 session had unacceptable segmentation (Appendix B.3). In these cases, the neuroradiologist manually extracted the linear measurements for the rejected session.
59 p In the remaining 12% of cases (6 patients), the automated outcomes required complete revision by the neuroradiologist during the preparation of the CAS-MDTM. This occurred when at least 2 sessions had unacceptable segmentations or mismatching linear measurements (Appendix B.4). In such instances, only the neuroradiologist’s manual extractions were used in the MDTM.
60 p Both the SS-MDTM and CAS-MDTM preparations placed a “somewhat high” workload on the neuroradiologist with CAS-MDTM preparation having a higher workload compared to SS-MDTM preparation (NASA-TLX [NASA Task Load Index] 45.5 vs 48, cf “Simulated MDTMs” in “Methods” section).
61 title Simulated MDTMs
62 p In the SS-MDTM, 7/50 patients were referred for active treatment including 5 for SRS and 2 for surgery. Thirty-nine patients were placed under surveillance and 4 were discharged. Patients under surveillance were imaged in line with our published protocol.4
63 p In the CAS-MDTM, 6 patients were referred for active treatment discussions, including 5 for SRS and 1 for surgery. Thirty-eight patients were placed under surveillance and 6 were discharged. In 2/50 patients, a surgical intervention was recommended in the SS-MDTM, while it was only recommended in 1/50 patients in the CAS-MDTM.

67 title Discussion
68 p In this study, we introduce a novel approach, CAS-MDTM, that integrates automated imaging biomarkers reports into VS clinical management. We validate this concept in a controlled simulated clinical setting, involving a multidisciplinary team of clinical experts. Through deep learning-based automated segmentation, we provide highly sensitive volume measurements, crucial for analyzing VS growth. This approach has the potential to streamline decision-making, enhancing clinical efficiency, and offers potential for more personalized patient care. The use of automated reporting resulted in a substantial improvement in clinical efficiency and the potential to enhance patient management quality.
69 p To the best of our knowledge, our research represents the first clinical deployment of an AI supported report for tumor management, where we examine its effect on clinical workflow and decision-making process. Our study complies with the Checklist for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging.24 Hawkins et al25 recently implemented a machine learning-based clinical workflow to perform segmentation, volumetric calculations, and generate reports using longitudinal MRI scans for low-grade glioma. However, their study did not explore how this technology could be integrated into clinical decision-making.
70 p During preparations for the CAS-MDTM, the neuroradiologist manually extracted linear measurements when the whole tumor segmentation was unacceptable at any of the 3 time points (index, second most recent, and most recent).
71 p We identified 4 scenarios contributing to faulty segmentations (Figure 4). Figure 4A visualizes a session with an oversegmentation of a small tumor, while Figure 4B and C depicts instances of undersegmentation and nonrecognition by the segmentation model, respectively. In such instances, the neuroradiologist manually extracted the linear measurements for these cases. Additionally, Figure 4D is an example of a session that was oversegmented, thus failing to provide an acceptable intra-/extrameatal boundary.

(C) A slice where the model fails to detect the tumor entirely; the true tumor location is shown by the manual annotation in red. (D) A slice with oversegmentation and an incorrect delineation of the boundary between the intrameatal and extrameatal tumor regions.
73 p During SS-MDTM preparations, the neuroradiologist chose between DWT and DEM, based on whether the maximum extrameatal dimension appeared larger than the porus on axial images. If the neuroradiologist was seeking serial comparable dimensions and the initial tumor was intrameatal, subsequent scans were interpreted using whole tumor volume measurements, even in the presence of a significant extrameatal component. This posed a significant challenge in the context of the automated imaging biomarker report, as we selected DEM according to our algorithm (Appendix A.3).
74 p For several cases, the whole tumor volume tended to provide more reliable observations on growth, as shown in Figure 5. Figure 5A displays postoperative yearly scans between 2011 and 2013, along with corresponding DWT and whole tumor volume measurements. The change between the second and third time points indicates definitive growth (a change in volume of over 20%), while the change in linear measurement (DWT) suggests equivocal growth.

(A) A case where changes in tumor volume clearly indicate growth, whereas linear measurements alone do not show a definitive increase. (B) A case with an irregular and inconsistent intrameatal and extrameatal boundary, making linear size measurements less reliable; in this scenario, volume measurement provides a more accurate assessment of tumor change.
76 p Differences in tumor boundaries between longitudinal scans was another reason for choosing whole tumor volume as the comparative metric for some patients. Figure 5B presents longitudinal scans of a post-SRS patient from 2012, 2016, and 2019 who had undergone SRS in 2005. Due to the irregular shape of the tumor, the separation of the intra-/extrameatal regions does not accurately depict the tumor’s behavior over time. These observations were highlighted by the neuroradiologist during the preparations and also when presenting to the MDTM.
77 p Contrary to expectations, our results demonstrated that the average preparation time for the CAS-MDTM was slightly longer than for the SS-MDTM (not statistically significant). This was partly due to the learning curve experienced by the neuroradiologist, which might have been mitigated through training on a separate trial cohort. Moreover, when preparing for the CAS-MDTM, the neuroradiologist was assessing the validity of both the tumor segmentations and linear/volume measurements, which was different to the SS-MDTM preparations that exclusively utilized linear measurements. The information overload on the summary report may have also contributed to the extended preparation time and the high preparation workload in the CAS-MDTM.
78 p The neuroradiologist’s preparation may also have been negatively affected by poor performance of the segmentation model. This may be a result of various factors including limited availability of the desired MRI sequences, nonstandard MRI acquisition, case complexity, tumor heterogeneity, the presence of very small tumors or residual tumor following surgery. Better automated segmentation results are likely to be achieved through the standardization of MRI sequences used to image VS and/or diversification of the training dataset. Nevertheless, minor adjustments will almost certainly be required in some difficult cases so an integrated interactive segmentation module, allowing the neuroradiologist to make real-time adjustments in the segmentation masks, should be developed before such technology can be fully integrated into the routine clinical workflow. Integrating such a module into PACS would further reduce the cognitive load of processing/visualizing various metrics, enabling the neuroradiologist to filter and focus on a specific preferred metric.
79 p The total number of discharge decisions were higher in the CAS-MDTM (6 patients) compared to the SS-MDTM (4 patients). The clinical multidisciplinary team (MDT) agreed to discharge 3 of the same patients in both MDTMs. One patient discharged from the SS-MDTM was not discharged from the CAS-MDTM; 3 additional patients were discharged from the CAS-MDTM. Discharged patients typically included those in old age (>80 years) with small stable tumors. Figure 3C summarizes the similarities and differences between the SS-MDTM and the CAS-MDTM.
80 p In the SS-MDTM, of 39 patients for whom surveillance imaging was originally recommended for actual patient care, the rescan interval increased for 11 patients (28.2%) decreased for 8 patients(20.5%), and remained unchanged for 16 patients (41%) as compared with the MDTs original clinical decision. Figure 3B illustrates how decisions taken in an SS-MDTM can change over time based on the original decisions made and the simulated MDTM decisions for the 50 patients. Of note, in the 3 patients where there was a discrepancy in the recommendation for treatment between the 2 MDTMs, there was only a difference in the determination of tumor growth in 1 patient. Patient management may have changed since the patient’s original clinical MDTM due to evolving clinical management and variations in the composition of MDTM participants together with their individual biases toward different treatments.
81 p The use of computer-assisted reporting enabled the MDT to offer patients a personalized management approach beyond standard surveillance protocols. Decision-making in both SS-MDTM and CAS-MDTM was primarily based on tumor size measurements. However, other factors such as the patient’s age and treatment history significantly influenced the decisions. In future studies, further exploration of these decision discrepancies is also essential to better understand how clinical judgment, patient-specific factors, and AI-assisted insights interact to influence management choices.
82 p Qualitative feedback obtained from the MDT demonstrated that the graphical representations illustrating growth trends over patients’ entire surveillance program were immensely beneficial. The inclusion of additional volume data played a vital role in enhancing the precision of interval change assessments particularly when deciding whether or not to extend the interval between surveillance scans. Oncologists especially valued having whole tumor volume measurements available as this is the metric used when delivering radiotherapy—not just the extrameatal portion.
83 p From the neuroradiologist’s perspective, the full automated imaging biomarker report, with its multiple inputs (linear and volume measurements for every imaging timepoint), was more challenging to interpret compared to the standard approach, where only index, second most recent, and most recent imaging were used. Consequently, in the CAS-MDTM, observations were limited to the same 3 sessions to reduce complexity. Additionally, the neuroradiologist highlighted the importance of keeping an expert human-in-the-loop for the absence of thorough data verification may lead to clinicians misinterpreting critical information. Accordingly, the integration of AI-assisted tools into clinical workflows must be approached with a human-in-the-loop framework, where neuroradiologists and clinicians can interactively refine model outputs and provide oversight in complex cases. This approach will ensure that automated segmentation methods remain both reliable and adaptable to real-world clinical scenarios and also foster trust among clinicians, ensuring that these tools effectively support decision-making rather than introducing new sources of uncertainty and AI hallucinations. In both simulated MDTMs, the neuroradiologist also provided observations on additional radiological features such as cystic changes, peritumoral edema, and contrast enhancement patterns. While tumor size and volume are key parameters in monitoring vestibular schwannomas, these qualitative features are equally important for a comprehensive assessment. Their evaluation underscores the continued value of expert neuroradiological interpretation, which offers clinical insights beyond the scope of current automated algorithms. This highlights the future need to incorporate quantitative biomarkers and visualizations capable of capturing a broader spectrum of tumor and brain abnormalities.
84 p We organized an online Patient Involvement focus group in partnership with the British Acoustic Neuroma Association to explore how patients could utilize this technology. We selected 12 individuals from a pool of over 200 interested patients across the United Kingdom, ensuring diversity in age, gender, and treatment experiences.
85 p This session provided valuable insights into patient preferences for automated reports, emphasizing the importance of visual and personalized formats. Patients highlighted the significance of clarity and simplicity in reporting. An artistic representation visually depicted the event, referencing the key components highlighted by the patients (Figure 6).
86 fig Figure 6.Visual illustration from the patient involvement session.Illustration summarizing feedback from the patient involvement session.
87 p The session highlighted how this report could be extended for use in combined MDTM clinics, as discussed in Colombo et al,26 where patients can access their personalized reports. This could improve workflow efficiency, patient-reported outcomes, decision transparency, and patient mental health.
88 p In conclusion, this is the first study to report the clinical deployment of an AI-supported reporting tool for tumor management. We introduced computer-assisted automated reporting exploiting deep learning-based segmentation to aid VS management and evaluated its impact in a simulated clinical environment. This work demonstrated a significant improvement in the efficiency of clinical MDTMs and highlights the positive impact computer-assisted reporting could have in delivering more personalized patient care.

"""Physical 3D inverse sampling around a preserved supervised training pivot."""
import numpy as np
import torch

def primitives(step,batch=2):
    rng=np.random.default_rng(np.random.SeedSequence([20261007,20261008,824,step]))
    return [dict(enabled=bool(rng.random()<.3),degrees_xyz=rng.uniform(-15,15,3).tolist(),scale=float(rng.uniform(.85,1.15))) for _ in range(batch)]

def pivots(geometry,shape_zrc):
    result=[];shape=np.asarray(shape_zrc)
    for g in geometry:
        if g['forced_foreground']:
            p=np.asarray(g['center'],float)-np.asarray(g['start'],float)
            for axis,flip in enumerate(g['flips']):
                if flip:p[axis]=shape[axis]-1-p[axis]
        else:p=(shape-1)/2
        assert np.all(p>=0) and np.all(p<shape)
        result.append(p.tolist())
    return result

def theta(record,pivot_zrc,spacing_zrc,shape_zrc):
    if not record['enabled']:return np.c_[np.eye(3),np.zeros(3)]
    ax,ay,az=np.deg2rad(record['degrees_xyz']);cx,cy,cz=np.cos([ax,ay,az]);sx,sy,sz=np.sin([ax,ay,az])
    rx=np.array([[1,0,0],[0,cx,-sx],[0,sx,cx]])
    ry=np.array([[cy,0,sy],[0,1,0],[-sy,0,cy]])
    rz=np.array([[cz,-sz,0],[sz,cz,0],[0,0,1]])
    rotation=rz@ry@rx
    spacing=np.asarray(spacing_zrc,float)[::-1];shape=np.asarray(shape_zrc,float)[::-1]
    a=np.diag(1/spacing)@rotation.T@np.diag(spacing)/record['scale']
    normalized=np.diag(2/shape)@a@np.diag(shape/2)
    pivot=2*(np.asarray(pivot_zrc)[::-1]+.5)/shape-1
    return np.c_[normalized,pivot-normalized@pivot]

def apply(x,y,records,pivot_zrc,spacing_zrc):
    assert x.dtype==y.dtype==np.float32 and x.shape==y.shape and x.ndim==5 and x.shape[1]==1
    assert len(x)==len(records)==len(pivot_zrc) and np.isin(y,[0,1]).all()
    xx=x.copy();yy=y.copy();matrices=[]
    for i,(p,pivot) in enumerate(zip(records,pivot_zrc)):
        matrix=theta(p,pivot,spacing_zrc,x.shape[2:]);matrices.append(matrix.tolist())
        if not p['enabled'] or (p['scale']==1 and not any(p['degrees_xyz'])):continue
        grid=torch.nn.functional.affine_grid(torch.from_numpy(matrix[None]),(1,1,*x.shape[2:]),align_corners=False)
        with torch.inference_mode():
            xx[i]=torch.nn.functional.grid_sample(torch.from_numpy(x[i:i+1].astype(np.float64)),grid,
                mode='bilinear',padding_mode='zeros',align_corners=False)[0].numpy().astype(np.float32)
            yy[i]=torch.nn.functional.grid_sample(torch.from_numpy(y[i:i+1].astype(np.float64)),grid,
                mode='nearest',padding_mode='zeros',align_corners=False)[0].numpy().astype(np.float32)
    assert np.isfinite(xx).all() and np.isin(yy,[0,1]).all()
